CSW is deeply concerned by the reintroduction of the Foreign Contribution Amendment Bill in India and its potential implications for the right to freedom of religion or belief. The proposed amendments would significantly expand state powers over assets acquired through foreign contributions. Under the bill, if an organization's FCRA registration expires, is cancelled, surrendered, or not renewed, a government-appointed authority could automatically take over, manage, or dispose of an NGO's assets. These powers can be carried out without prior independent judicial scrutiny. The bill also fails to differentiate what constitutes a foreign-funded asset. effectively treating entire domestic assets and their appreciated value as regulated foreign property. The absence of a clear definition regarding provisions prohibiting the use of foreign contributions for so-called proselytization also creates scope for arbitrary interpretation and application, raising serious concerns for religious organizations, humanitarian actors, and civil society groups engaged in legitimate faith-based activities. Across India, faith-based organisations provide essential services, including education, healthcare, disaster relief, and support for vulnerable communities. The prospect of losing control of these institutions because of administrative decisions relating to the FCRA registration has created considerable uncertainty and fear. We urge the Government of India and Members of Parliament to ensure that any legislation fully complies with India's international human rights obligations. protects civic space, and safeguards the fundamental rights to freedom of religion or belief for all. Thank you.

Thank you.

Human Rights Now strongly condemns U.S. sanctions on ICC personnel, most recently against President Tomoko Akane and Abdoulaye Sey from the Office of the Prosecutor. The U.S. has sanctioned over a dozen court personnel in all, including nine judges, two deputy prosecutors, and the former prosecutor. U.S. officials have been explicit that their goal is to systematically disable the ICC's ability to operate, and they have pressured other states to also reject it. The most recent sanctions form part of this campaign to destroy the court. The sanctions have severely impacted the recipients and their families' daily lives by seizing, canceling, or disabling their access to bank accounts, credit cards, financial services, and e-mail and social media accounts, among other restrictions. Many extraterritorial institutions overcomply with the sanctions from fear of penalty without legal requirement. These sanctions undermine the rule of law and the international legal order, flagrantly attack the court's judicial independence, and hinder it meeting its legal mandate and impede justice for victims. We call on ICC member states to urgently take effective and coordinated action to protect the Court, including through domestic and regional blocking legislation. We also call on member states to take action to protect other actors cooperating with the Court who have also been sanctioned, including the Special Rapporteur for Palestine and Palestinian NGOs. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the representative of Center for Inquiry, intervention by video.

Mr. President, 30 months behind bars for a t-shirt. This is the sentence handed down in Morocco to feminist activist Ibtissam Lajjar for wearing a t-shirt bearing a slogan deemed offensive. She was arrested, prosecuted and imprisoned under laws against offending Islam for peacefully expressing her views, while those who threatened her online with death and rape remain free. Also in Morocco, clerics have called for the killing of Dr. Mohammed Al-Faied over remarks that some considered insulting to Prophet Muhammad. In Algeria, novelist Kamel Daoud became the target of a campaign calling for his death after an imam accused him of apostasy. This is a glaring double standard, Mr. President. The law is wielded as a weapon against those who express peaceful opinions, while those who incite violence are tolerated. Freedom of belief is not complete unless it includes the freedom to be an atheist, and freedom of expression is not complete unless it includes the freedom to criticize the sacred. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the representative of European Center for Law and Justice, intervention by video.

Thank you, Mr. President. With over 3,000 Christians massacred in just eight months this year, the ongoing ethno-religious cleansing in Nigeria is a catastrophe. Fulani armed militias in the Middle Belt have become the deadliest perpetrators, even though media attention remains focused on Boko Haram. Christians are being systematically slaughtered and plundered across Kaduna, Benue and Plateau states, including Mangu, Dengdeng, Dorking, Nobi, Kum and Ryom, where two-year-old children are being mutilated by gunfire. Over 19,000 churches have been torched nationwide in 16 years. These terrorists are growing more complex in their threat, multiplying mass abductions and targeting schools. Their actions have forced closures across 11 states as they used children as human shields. Local dioceses are currently being asphyxiated by the financial targeting of the clergy through exorbitant ransoms. The inertia of the Nigerian government persists despite the proclaimed state of emergency. Therefore, the ECFJ calls on this Council To demand that the Nigerian government immediately deploy neutral security forces to protect churches, schools, and defenseless Christian villages, and to secure plundered agricultural lands. To appoint an independent investigation mechanism to break the systematic impunity enjoyed by these Islamist militias. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the representative of International Pro Bono Legal Services Association, Limited.

Excellencies, The situation in East Asia continues to demand the collective attention of the international community, not only in the global north, but also above all, the global south, which represents the majority of humanity. We are deeply concerned that Japan's current administration is engaging in war propaganda in violation of the commitment to Article 20 of the ICCPR by fearmongering and invoking Taiwan as a casus belli for war in the region. Efforts to hollow out Article 9 of the Japanese Constitution, together with the intensified militarization of the Ryukyu Islands, point to preparations for precisely such a conflict. These actions not only threaten the very stability of the entire East Asian region, but also risk repeating history by turning the island chain into a battleground, where a third of the indigenous Ryukyu population were sacrificed to buy time for the Imperial Japanese Army in 1945. We must not allow that tragedy to recur. Civil society organizations in the Republic of Korea, the Republic of Philippines, Hong Kong SAR, and elsewhere, once occupied and colonized by the Imperial Japanese forces, have voiced the same alarm. So too have anti-war protesters across Japan. War benefits none other than military-industrial complex and powers of the old order. If we fail to halt this military buildup, we risk triggering a conflict that could escalate into global war and create an existential crisis for the institution itself. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the representative of Franciscans International for a joint statement, intervention by video.

Mr. President, we express our ongoing concern regarding the deteriorating human rights situations of the indigenous populations of West Papua, Indonesia. Heavy military presence and ongoing security operations in Yahukimo, in Tanjayam, Maybrat, and Paniai are causing ongoing displacement. There is limited or no humanitarian access for IDP sheltering in forest or host communities. In July 2026, the Indonesian government acknowledged that around 122,000 civilians have been displaced due to conflicts in West Papua. Most IDPs are from Puncak, Intan Jaya, Nduga, and Maybrat, and live scattered across West Papua in the towns of Jayapura, Mimika, Nabire, Wamena, and Sorong. Their rights to life, security, work, health, education, housing, and food are being violated. Therefore, we call upon the Indonesian government to address the IDP situation with urgency and allow humanitarian aid without delay. We are also increasingly alarmed by the food and energy related national strategy project in South Papua, particularly in Merauke Regency. Over 40,000 indigenous Papuans are affected by the clearing of more than 2 million hectares of rainforest and swampland critical to their lives. We urge the Guinean government to immediately re-evaluate the national strategic project, pending a comprehensive environmental and social impact assessment, and conduct a free, prior and informed consent consultation process with indigenous communities. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the representative of Global Institute for Water, Environment and Health, intervention by video.

As then, climate change disproportionately affects developing countries where poverty, energy insecurity and climate vulnerability are closely interconnected. The transition to renewable energy must therefore be understood not only as a climate imperative, but also as an opportunity to advance human rights and the right to development. India's experience demonstrated how renewable energy expansion can contribute to rural electrification, reduce energy poverty, create a green employment, and strengthen sustainable livelihoods. By 2025, India had reached approximately 50% of installed power capacity from non-fossil fuel sources and is advancing toward 500 gigawatts by 2030. We encourage the Council and the international community to strengthen climate finance, facilitate non-discriminatory technology transfer, support just transitions, and expand cooperation on clean energy infrastructure. Climate action must be equitable, inclusive, and development-oriented. Renewable energy should become a pathway to realizing the rights to health, adequate living standards, livelihood, and sustainable development. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the representative of Kiam Rehabilitation Center for Victims of Torture.

Mr. President, there are grave violations of international law committed by Israel in southern Lebanon. First, those are detained and missing persons. Since October 2023, the ICRC was not able to visit any Lebanese citizen held by Israel, including fighters and civilians and many Lebanese families do not know the whereabouts of their children or loved ones or to know about their living conditions and despite the release of a number of civilians others were abducted there are reports that indicate that 35 people who were detained in 2023 continue to exist in Israel there are also dozens who continue to be unaccounted for and they are deprived of the right to visit in accordance to article 49 of Geneva Fourth Convention. Israel also has killed 370 children, and this is a disregard of the distinction between military and civilian objects. Israel also has razed dozens of villages in the border area and also destroyed olive farms and it disregards the principle of the prohibition of collective punishment. We call on the Council to request Israel to allow the ICRC to visit Lebanese detainees and to stop its attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure in Lebanon, and also to condemn Israel for its treatment of prisoners. Thank you.
I give the floor to the representative of International Carrier Support Association.

Mr. Vice President, we are deeply concerned about the prolonged detention of former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte. President Duterte, now 81 years old, was arrested on 11 March 2025 and surrendered to the ICC custody in Hague. He has now spent 560 days in detention while his trial is scheduled only 30 November 2026. Article 9 of ICCPR protects individuals from arbitrary detention and requires the pre-trial detention not becomes indefinite. Article 14 guarantees the presumption of innocence and the rights to trial without undue delay. We are also concerned about the principle of complementarity under Article 17 of the Rome Statute. The Philippines has a functioning judicial system with multiple levels. The ICC should intervene only when the national authorities are genuinely unwilling or unable to investigate or prosecute. The circumstances surrounding President Duterte's arrest and surrender appears deeply entangled with the domestic political conflicts between the Marcos and Duterte political camps. International justice must never become an instrument in a domestic political struggle. We urge this Council to examine the legality and human rights implications of the President's prolonged detention, including the age and health, and to call for a full respect for due process, judicial independence, and the presumption of innocence. Justice must be independent from politics. Thank you, Vice-President.
Thank you. I give the floor to the representative of East and Horn of Africa Human Rights Defenders Project.

Mr. Vice President, we are concerned about the dangerous narrative fed by a cynical use of the UN financial crisis and a selective reading of the HRC's mandate, whereby mechanisms that do not enjoy the consent of the country concerned are illegitimate. Yet, UNGA resolution 62/51 is clear. Alongside dialogue, engagement and technical support, the Council has a responsibility to address human rights violations, including gross and systematic violations. Item 4 is one of the ways the Council discharges its mandate. Where violations are politically motivated and states lack the will to improve their record, the Council's role is to help generate political will by ensuring scrutiny, condemning violations, and increasing the political cost of abuses. Vice President, we are deeply concerned by events in the Sahel, Burkina Faso, and Mali and Niger. The Human Rights Council have a role to play in the documentation of these violations and the protection of the civilian population. Turning now to the DRC, we urge the High Commissioner to do his utmost to ensure the implementation of the relevant Security Council resolutions. The Commission of Inquiry in Kivu needs to be fully operationalized as soon as possible so that it can discharge on its mandate. We urge the international community to pay close attention to South Sudan as the country is preparing for its first ever national elections without key prerequisites being met. risks of relapse into large-scale conflict are increasing. Thank you.
I give the floor to the representative of Gulf Center for Human Rights Limited.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. The Gulf Center for Human Rights and Al-Qusd for Human Rights wish to draw attention to recent developments in Yemen and the execution crisis in Saudi Arabia. The recent escalation of hostilities in Yemen has led to significant advances by the Houthis, which impact the conflict locally as well as the wider hostilities in the region. Initial reports indicate that significant violations have occurred as territory changes hands. This conflict, since 2014, has seen widespread human violations by all parties to the conflict. Clear international pressure for accountability has shown to be effective pressure to reduce abuses. The response of the Human Rights Council has moved from an effective group of eminent experts started in 2017, but not renewed in 2021, to the current item 10 resolution, which currently barely implies a need for accountability and does not call for an interactive dialogue, thereby leaving this context essentially unaddressed. There is an urgent need for this Council to do better. In Saudi Arabia, the use of the death penalty is a growing crisis with an international component, with foreign nationals bearing the brunt. Since the beginning of 2024, Saudi authorities have carried out at least 860 executions, with non-lethal drug-related executions making up over half and disproportionately affecting foreign nationals from Asian and African countries, notably Somalia, Ethiopia, Pakistan, Egypt, and Nigeria. Testimonies have confirmed a pattern of abuse suffered in the course of their arrest, detention, and trial, including a lack of access to consular support, legal representation, and adequate interpretation in court documents. The use of the death penalty in violation of international human rights law heightens fears. Thank you.
I give the floor to the representative of Americans for Democracy and Human Rights in Bahrain, Incorporated. Intervention by video.

Mr. President, we draw the Council's attention to Bahrain's escalating use of nationality revocation to suppress dissent, particularly amid the recent war with Iran and continuing a pattern since 2012. On the 27th of April 2026, Bahrain's Ministry of Interior revoked the nationality of 69 people, including some family members, over alleged sympathy for Iranian attacks or collusion with foreign entities, all without judicial proceedings to establish these allegations. A decree was also issued removing judicial oversight of nationality revocation decisions and denying those affected the right to challenge or appeal them. Three MPs were also excluded from Parliament after opposing the decree. Bahrain's use of nationality to punish expression or dissent and its denial of judicial safeguards raises serious concerns about discrimination, statelessness, and the denial of effective remedies. We call on the Council to pressure Bahrain to stop arbitrary nationality revocations, ensure affected individuals can challenge them and seek judicial review, restore the nationality of those stripped of it, and reinstate the three MPs to their seats. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the representative of Beijing and Jiu Association for International Exchanges.

Mr. Vice President, Hong Kong is a society underpinned by the rule of law and has always adhered to the principle that laws must be obeyed and lawbreakers held accountable. The rights and freedoms enjoyed by Hong Kong residents are well protected under the Basic Law, the National Security Law, and Hong Kong Bills of Rights Ordinance, which ensures that the provisions of the ICCPR and ICESCR as applied to Hong Kong are upheld in accordance with the law. Furthermore, the National Security Law and the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance clearly stipulates that the principle of the rule of law shall be adhered to in preventing, suppressing, and imposing punishments for offenses endangering national security. Any suggestions that certain persons should be immune from legal consequences for their illegal act is no different from advocating a special privilege to break the law, and this totally runs against the spirit of the rule of law. The defendants of national security cases were put on trial, not because of their political views or beliefs. All defendants received a fair trial in accordance with the laws of Hong Kong, free from any interference. Organizations should not interfere in ongoing legal proceedings in Hong Kong courts, nor should they interfere with Hong Kong's judicial independence in accordance with the rule of law. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the representative of Organization for Defending Victims of Violence, intervention by video.

Mr. President, we urge the Human Rights Council and its mechanisms to strengthen scrutiny and accountability regarding the United States' compliance with international human rights obligations, including its actions beyond borders. First, we call on the High Commissioner and relevant special procedures to strengthen monitoring and reporting on human rights impacts of US policies and actions, including unilateral coercive measures, military operations, and external interventions. Second, we urge States to use the UPR to raise specific and measurable questions concerning US compliance with international human rights obligations, including the extraterritorial and humanitarian consequences of its policies. Third, continued non-cooperation with UPR or other UN human rights mechanisms should not result in reduced scrutiny. We therefore support a dedicated Council debate on persistent non-cooperation. Fourth, we call on the greater attention to state responsibility for violations beyond national borders, including where violations are facilitated through military actions, arms transfers, political support, or coercive economic measures. Finally, we urge the Council to apply human rights scrutiny consistently to all the states, regardless of their political, economic, or military power. No state should avoid meaningful scrutiny or accountability through political influence or non-cooperation. I thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the representative of Amnesty International.

Mr. Vice President, as detailed in a major report issued last week, we have exposed how the Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity to crush the Women, Life, Freedom uprising, unlawfully killing hundreds of protesters and bystanders, persecuting their families, and subjecting thousands to arbitrary detention and forced disappearance or torture. These crimes were carried out as part of a widespread and systematic attack against the civilian population pursuant to a state policy. We urge the establishment of an international criminal justice mechanism and referral to the International Criminal Court. Egypt continues to face an arbitrary detention crisis, with thousands behind bars solely for exercising their rights to freedom of expression, association, and peaceful assembly. We urge their immediate release, including the release of human rights lawyer Ibrahim Metwally, who has been arbitrarily detained for eight years solely for his human rights activism and for engaging with this Council. Security forces arrested him at Cairo airport while he was on his way to Geneva to discuss enforced disappearances in Egypt. He is now facing three separate trials on unfounded charges, some of which carry the death penalty as a possible sentence. We are alarmed by a presidential directive issued in Algeria to amend the penal code and broaden the use of the death penalty in the aftermath of devastating wildfires. We urge the Algerian authorities to immediately abandon any plans to expand the scope of the death penalty or to resume executions. On Ethiopia, we remain deeply concerned by rising violence in Tigray amid ongoing conflicts in the Amhara and Oromia regions, with grave risk of continued serious and widespread human rights violations. We urge this Council's continued monitoring and reporting. Thank you.
I give the floor to the representative of Women Human Rights International Association.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. To conceal its past crimes, the Islamic Republic of Iran and its judiciary have demolished prisons, built parking lots over victims' burial sites, and constructed roads and highways over mass grave. Through these actions, they have sought to destroy evidence and erase the crimes from Iran's collective memory. Gohardasht Prison is a symbol of execution and torture in Iran's prison during the 1980s, particularly the 1988 massacres of political prisoners. In July 2024, former UN Special Rapporteur Javed Rehman characterized the massacre as the crime against humanity and genocide. Yet this effort has failed. Despite the passage of decades and the increasing use of execution to suppress opponents and terrorize society, true and justice remain central demands of the Iranian people. Preserving Gohar Dasht prison and the mass graves means defending families' right to know the truth and obtain justice. We call on the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran and the Special Rapporteur on Human Rights in Iran to act urgently to halt this destruction, preserve evidence, conduct independent investigation, and hold those who ordered and carry out these crimes accountable. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the representative of China Ethnic Minorities Association for External Exchanges.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. We've long focused on human rights, especially the human rights of ethnic minorities. We believe the right to substance and the right to development are inalienable fundamental human rights. Our visit to Xinjiang showed us this firsthand. Last year was the 70th anniversary of the establishment of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region. Over 70 years of development, the region's GDP grew from 1.2 billion to 2.1 trillion yuan. Life expectancy rose from around 30 to 77 years. More than 3 million rural poor people were lifted out of poverty. The Tian Shan Shengli Tunnel, the world's longest expressway tunnel, cut travel time across the Tian Shan Mountains from over three hours to about 20 minutes. People of all ethnic groups are sharing in the benefits of development. That's human rights in the truest sense. But in many parts of the world, these rights are still being violated. The United States, for its own selfish interests, has imposed sanctions and stopped conflict in the Middle East, killing tens of thousands of civilians. Putting hegemony above people's right to life is a cancer on the international human rights horse, and we must firmly resist it. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the representative of Medical Support Association for Underprivileged Iranian Patients, intervention by video.

Mr. President, when we talk about war, we picture rubble, soldiers, bombs, but there's another kind of victim we hardly see, the invisible victims of war. These are patients nowhere near the battlefield. Their harm comes from the collapse around them. No medicine, no blood, no ambulance, no electricity. A system fails and a life quietly slips away. So here's the question. Does protecting the right to life and health stop at keeping hospitals standing? Or does it have to cover the whole chain of treatment? The pills, the blood banks, the ambulances, the power lines, the phone signals, the doctors and nurses who never make it to work. Because for some patients, time is treatment. Delay isn't just inconvenient, it's fatal physical harm. And the law should address it. When we judge an attack, we can't ignore its ripple effects on health. A condition that could be managed must never be allowed to spiral into a life or death emergency. Mr. President, we call on the Special Rapporteur on the right to health to document impact of US and Israeli aggression on Iranians lives and health the direct casualties as well as the deaths and injuries resulting from disruptions to medical care thank you
thank you I give the floor to the representative of JESOR youth organization

Mr. President, I wish to make an urgent appeal on behalf of Dr. Sabiha Baloch, as I stay with the Baloch Yakeety Committee. Dr. Sabiha said in a court, "I fear that I may be arrested, forcibly disappeared, or even killed for speaking about the suffering of my people. Five of my colleagues are already in prison for peacefully speaking about human rights violation. I've been part of the same peaceful struggle, and I fear I could be next. Before I become another victim, I ask the international community, please look to what Barashistan now, not after another life is lost. The Barash Yekiti Committee is a peaceful grassroots movement. Its leader, including Dr. Marang Barash and Sibir Chaji, are serving life sentences following proceedings that have raised serious concerns about the process. According to PYC documentation, 1,223 enforced disappearances and 188 extrajudicial killings were recorded in 2025. Civilians, including children, have also reportedly lost their lives during military operation. I urgently appeal to the United Nations to investigate the human rights situation in Balochistan and urge Pakistan to address enforced disappearances and protect civilians and human rights defenders and ensure justice and accountability. Please, act before another voice is silenced. End of quote. Thank you, Mr. President.
Thank you. I give the floor to the representative of Centre Europe.

President, my name is Jaime Guantacudo and I'm the spokesperson of the Mapuche Collective and I'd like to draw the attention of the Human Rights Council to the human rights situation in Chile, more specifically to the systematic violation of the collective rights of the Mapuche people, a violation carried out by the Chilean state. We denounce the militarization of the Mapuche territory, a process that's been going on for more than 4.5 years. We also use this, uh, august body to denounce the seizure of the historic leader of Temecuiqui, Jorge Juan Chulum, by the… Chilean exercise in a violent repressive operation of war, denominated Operation Trident, which demonstrates in Chile there is political persecution of ancestral Mapuche leaders and authorities. We call for the release of all Mapuche political prisoners. We also call upon the government of Chile to cease the reform projects that are currently going through Congress. Uh, as part of which they are seeking first to modify the indigenous law, allowing indigenous land to be sold, leased, mortgaged, which would lead to the social, cultural, political, and land breakdown of the Mapuche people. They're also using the national posters to try and put forward a constitutional reform project on public safety, which would affect not just the fundamental rights of the Mapuche people, but the entire Chilean civilian population. To conclude, we urge this Council to request the Chilean State to effectively comply with all those international instruments that it has ratified, as well as to ensure the respect and protection of the collective rights of the Mapuche people. Thank you very much.
Thank you. I give the floor to the representative of Al-Bashir Foundation for Development.

We are determined to uphold the right to self-determination. It's vital that the right to self-determination be exercised and that there be space to exercise same, and that an end be put to the aggression and attacks on activists and defenders who are claiming such rights, particularly for the Sarawak people. President, we feel compelled to take the floor because the areas of Western Sahara under occupation live these violations of the rights on a daily basis, and the international human rights protection architecture mechanisms is unable to exercise its functions in a territory which under the control of another power. We're deprived of our rights, including, for example, the right to electricity and power, which is a fundamental right. The Maghreb occupying forces deprive of this right and many others as well. Up until very recently, the Sahrawi had been deprived of the right to exercise various other rights. One of our lawyers and representatives and many other Sahrawi defenders are imprisoned when championing and advocating for our range of rights. We are talking here about a territory under occupation and that needs to be recognized. We cannot turn our back on what's happening there. The international community should not demonstrate indifference to what's happening in this occupied territory. And so we call upon you, President, and this Human Rights Council to pay more attention to this region of the world. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the representative of British Humanist Association, intervention by video.

We are deeply concerned by the implications of the Kishinev Declaration adopted by the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe, not only for the human rights protections of migrants, refugees and asylum seekers, but for the principle of universality. Weakening the rights of some risks undermining the rights of everyone. As a non-binding political declaration, it reflects a broader climate that is increasingly hostile to migrants. Countries such as Denmark and the UK have recently introduced legislation that purports to limit the application of convention rights amid misrepresentations in reporting that the European Court of Human Rights obstructs the deportation of foreign national offenders. This is despite the court already having an extremely limited impact on national migration and asylum decisions. Over the last 10 years, just 2% of the just under half a million applications submitted to the court concerned immigration. Of those, the Court ruled against states in just 6% of cases. We are unclear about the purpose of the declaration. The Court already provides a mechanism for dialogue. Protocol 16 allows high courts of state parties to obtain advisory opinions from the Court. Yet, despite the Kishinev Declaration itself encouraging states to consider ratifying Protocol 16, some countries that supported the process leading to the declaration, such as the UK and Denmark, have not done so. We call on European states to ratify Protocol 16 and to utilize its advisory function as a means of engaging in open, informed, and constructive dialogue that the Kishinau Declaration calls for. Thank you.
I give the floor to the representative of JAMI, Hiyagaran, Teb, Sonati, Vasalamat, Iranian intervention by video.

infrastructure is not limited to hospital buildings. The health and well-being of civilians also depend on a safe environment, clean water, safe soil, and access to safe food and medicinal resources. The bombings of oil storage facilities in Tehran and Karaj does not end with the destruction of physical infrastructure. Such attacks can contaminate air, soil, and water, seriously disrupting the environmental foundations of public health, with potentially lasting consequences. We must distinguish between visible destruction and invisible contamination. An environment may appear intact while its soil or water has been contaminated, rendering plants and natural resources unsafe for food or medicinal use. Moreover, the end of an attack does not necessarily mean the end of its harm. Certain environmental impacts and health consequences may emerge months or even years later, potentially affecting future generations. We therefore call on the Special Rapporteur on the Implications of Human Rights of the Environmentally Sound Management and and disposal of hazardous substances and wastes, and the Special Rapporteur on the Right to Food to assess the impacts of the military operations conducted by the US and Israel, including their foreseeable and long-term environmental consequences. Where harm is established, remedy must, where necessary, include environmental cleanup, restoration, and ecological rehabilitation. I thank you.
Thank you. Women, I give the floor to the representative of Women and Sea Committee for CSW, Sida.

Dear Chair, for more than four decades, the authorities in Islamic Republic of Iran have violated the fundamental rights of women through gender apartheid, compulsory hijab, and institutionalized misogyny. We must not forget that thousands of women political prisoners were executed in 1980s. According to human rights organizations, more than 1,000 people have executed in Iran in 2026 alone, including at least 22 women. The authorities increasingly use the death penalty to silence dissent and spread fear. Eight women, including Zahra Tabari and 24 years old, are currently under death sentence for political reason and face imminent execution. This issue is deeply personal to me. My cousin, Fatemeh Khamaleh, was executed in Karaj in August 2026. Her case highlights serious concern regarding due process, access to justice, and discrimination against women in Iran's judicial system. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the representative of Alliance Defending Freedom.

Mr. Vice-President, The human right to freedom of expression sits at the very heart of any free and democratic society. It is therefore extremely concerning that the United Kingdom, a vocal proponent of this right in international fora, has seen that very freedom rapidly undermined for its own populace through the imposition of vague and overbroad laws enabling widespread state censorship and surveillance. National Civil Society reports that over 62,000 people have been arrested for alleged communications offenses over the past five years, to say nothing of the many thousands more subjected to questioning and investigation for actions as simple as viewing a social media post. Laws such as the Online Safety Act grant authorities sweeping powers to monitor and crack down on digital content deemed harmful according to arbitrary and subjective standards. So-called buffer zone legislation is being used to criminalise offers of consensual conversation and even silent prayer in public places. Just last year, a 75-year-old grandmother was arrested and criminally charged in Scotland merely for standing outside a hospital in a buffer zone, peacefully holding a sign that read, "Coercion is a crime. Here to talk, only if you want." Mr. Vice President, the existential impact of such laws restricting freedom of expression, including their chilling effect on society, cannot be overstated. We call on the UK government to urgently change course and take action to restore the fundamental freedoms of its people. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the representative of Union of Disabled People Organization of Azerbaijan. I understand they're absent. I'll give the floor to the representative of Human Rights Watch.

Mr. President, 10 years since abuses escalated against Uyghurs in Xinjiang, the Chinese government crackdown remains severe. This Council should convene a dedicated discussion to follow up on the recommendations of the OHCHR assessment report, which concluded that grave abuses in Xinjiang may constitute crimes against humanity, and should also address repression across China, including in Tibet and Hong Kong, and persecution of religious minorities. We share the concern of the fact-finding mission on Venezuela that the repressive machinery that has sustained political persecution and facilitated grave human rights violations remains operational. Impunity continues while some of those the fact-finding mission found reasonable grounds to believe responsible for crimes against humanity and other serious violations remain in key positions of power. Notwithstanding the release of some political prisoners and decrease in certain forms of repression, hundreds of people are still arbitrarily detained while abusive laws that have enabled repression remain in place. Our position remains unequivocal. Sustained international engagement based on objective, independent human rights investigations is essential in this fragile moment. We therefore call on States to support the two-year renewal of the FFM, whose work can guide and support such engagement. We regret the closure of the confidential complaint against Tajikistan under the Council's complaint procedure, as the government continues its severe and wide-ranging crackdown on political opponents, dissidents, journalists and human rights defenders inside the country and beyond its borders, and as systematic repression of ethnic minorities continues. We appeal to this Council to convene an open meeting with the participation of victims. Thank you.
I give the floor to the representative of Focus Asia Foundation.

Mr. Vice President, we remain deeply alarmed by the persistent and widespread practice of enforced disappearances in Pakistan. Families continue to wait, sometimes for years, for any news of loved ones taken by the state forces. The Commission of Inquiry on Enforced Disappearances has failed to deliver accountability or even reliable information. Pakistan must criminalize enforced disappearances in domestic law, ratify the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearances, and allow the Working Group on Enforced unhindered access. We are equally troubled by the systematic curtailment of the right to freedom of peaceful assembly. Peaceful protesters face mass arrests and sweeping charges under anti-terrorism and cyber crimes. We condemn the arbitrary detention of Dr. Mehran Baloch and other Baloch activists who have been targeted for peacefully demanding truth and justice, further disappeared. We call for her immediate and unconditional release and for the dropping of all charges arising from peaceful advocacy. We further urge Pakistan to impose an immediate moratorium on the death penalty. We call on the Council to maintain dedicated monitoring of Pakistan for concrete, time-bound reforms. The victims deserve more than statements. They deserve action. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the representative of Chinese Association for International Understanding, intervention by video.

Thank you, Mr. President. We appreciate the expert mechanism for its study on artificial intelligence, cultural rights, and the right to development. We share the study's central insight Existing international human rights law already provides a solid foundation for governing AI, and the right to development offers a people-centered framework to guide it. What is needed now is to translate these forms into coherent international standards, so that innovation helps close global divides rather than creating new ones. The Chinese Association for International Understanding has long fostered dialogue among legal scholars from different countries, and grounding the common values of humanity in the rule of law.
